The app sends a POST request exactly to the address in the “Server address” field, path and parameters included. The request body is the whole backup file, with no multipart or JSON wrapping. Content type is application/octet-stream, the length is known in advance and sent in Content-Length. Both http and https work; the app waits up to a minute for an answer.

X-Backup-Name — a file name to save the backup under: remember-YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM plus the backup extension. The time is the phone’s. Don’t use the name as a path: the server should strip everything except letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore.
Authorization: Bearer and the token — only if a token is set in the app. The server compares it with its own and answers 401 without saving if it doesn’t match.

Any 2xx code (200, 201, 204) means the backup is saved: the app records the time in “Last backup on the server”. The response body is not read. Any other code or a lost connection is an error: its text shows under the button, and a scheduled attempt is retried later.

The same file as a manual export: the database, its key and photos, encrypted with the backup password. The server can’t and shouldn’t read it — only store it. Restore it with a regular import in the app, using the same password. Every upload is a new full file; the server removes old ones itself if needed.

Manually — with “Send a backup now”. On schedule — once every given number of days, when the phone has a network; Android picks the exact time to save battery, so a backup may arrive a few hours late. If it fails, the system retries later by itself.

The backup is always encrypted, so its contents can’t be seen even over http. But over http the token is visible on the network — use https for a server reachable from the internet. The backup password and token are stored on the phone, encrypted with a key from its chip.
